name: Refugee / Asylum Status (ad hoc administrative arrangement)

requirements.blocker_text: Fled persecution, conflict, or a comparable protection need in the country of origin -- Bangladesh has no codified refugee-definition statute, so this is modeled at the general internationally-recognized standard rather than a Bangladesh-specific legal test.

The government must have exercised its discretionary power under Section 10 of the Foreigners Act, 1946 to exempt the applicant's 'class or description of foreigner' from the Act's ordinary provisions -- protection here is administered class-by-class at government discretion, not through an individual legal right to apply.

evidence_required.document: Registration with camp/administrative authorities (for populations covered by an active exemption order)

outcome.duration_length: not defined by statute -- varies by the terms of the specific administrative exemption order in force for a given population

sources.title: UNHCR Rights Mapping and Analysis Platform (RIMAP) -- Bangladesh: 'In absence of any refugee/asylum legislation at domestic level, the Foreigner's Act [1946] remains the key legislation regulating the Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh'; Section 3 gives the government broad power to regulate foreigners' entry/presence, Section 10 allows exempting any 'class or description of foreigner' from the Act, which is how refugee populations are administratively managed

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Bangladesh). STATUS: DRAFT -- tier-2 UNHCR-hosted analysis is the clearest source located; the underlying Foreigners Act, 1946 itself is a colonial-era general alien-control statute, not a purpose-built refugee law, and was not independently located at tier-1 in this build. THE SINGLE MOST STRIKING STRUCTURAL FINDING IN THIS BANGLADESH BUILD, WORTH STATING PLAINLY: Bangladesh hosts what is widely reported as the world's largest refugee camp complex (Cox's Bazar, over a million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar) with NO codified domestic refugee or asylum law of any kind -- protection is administered entirely through discretionary government exemption orders under a 1946 colonial statute originally designed for routine foreigner regulation, not refugee protection, plus ad hoc bilateral/UNHCR coordination arrangements. This is structurally different from every other humanitarian route built so far in this dataset: Rwanda, Ethiopia, and Nigeria all have purpose-built domestic refugee statutes with formal eligibility committees and appeal mechanisms (even if imperfectly resourced); Bahrain and Myanmar (as built) have essentially no framework and no meaningful refugee population; Bangladesh sits in a third category entirely -- large-scale, long-term, real protection extended to enormous numbers of people, but through administrative discretion rather than codified legal entitlement. This is disclosed as a structural finding, not asserted as either better or worse than a codified system -- it is simply a materially different legal architecture that anyone relying on this route needs to understand before treating it as a predictable, rules-based process the way bd_citizenship_naturalisation.json or bd_work_permit.json are.
